title: Apple's Big iPhone Event Had One Glaring Omission: The iPhone 18
summary:
Apple's annual iPhone launch is usually a predictable affair: new standard model, new Pro model, maybe a surprise or two. But this year, the company pulled a fast one. During yesterday's stream, Apple unveiled its first foldable phone — the passport-shaped iPhone Duo — along with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, new AirPods, and new Apple Watches. Notice what's missing? The plain old iPhone 18.

That's right. For the first time since Apple started making 'Pro' phones in 2019, the company did not launch a standard and Pro iPhone at the same time. If you were planning to upgrade to a regular new iPhone this fall, you're out of luck — unless you settle for an iPhone 17.

So where is the iPhone 18? According to reports from The Information, MacRumors, and others, Apple will likely announce a second set of iPhones next spring. That would almost certainly include the iPhone 18, plus possible follow-ups like the iPhone Air 2 or a budget-friendly iPhone 18e. The standard iPhone remains the most popular option, accounting for 6 percent of smartphone sales in Q2 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Apple probably won't leave those fans high and dry for long.

Why would Apple delay its most popular phone? A few reasons. First, Apple now makes six iPhones. Promoting them all at once — while also pushing new AirPods and Watches — would be a daunting task. Second, there's an AI-driven component crunch pushing tech prices upward. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cost $1,199 and $1,299, respectively — $100 more than last year's models. By holding off on a new standard iPhone, Apple lets the pricier Pro models take the heat. Folks interested in the Pros or the Duo are less likely to skip an upgrade than budget-conscious standard buyers.

As for whether standard iPhone fans will feel left out, that depends. The iPhone 18 Pro has some impressive upgrades, especially in AI compute performance. There's also an enhanced Dynamic Island — that little black bar at the top of the screen — which can now show info from up to three apps at once. Camera improvements are expected too. But there's no single game-changing feature that screams 'must-have.'

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available for pre-order from Apple on Saturday, September 12, and hit stores September 18, 2026. The iPhone Duo pre-order starts October 16, ahead of an October 23 launch. As for the iPhone 18? We'll just have to wait for Apple to say more.
why_it_matters: Apple's decision shows how consumer technology now works: when AI-driven demand raises the cost of parts, those costs get passed to buyers, and companies manage the squeeze by launching premium models first and cheaper ones later. For teenagers who will soon buy their own devices, it means the entry-level iPhone is becoming a later option rather than a cheaper one, and that what appears on stage at a launch event is shaped by supply chains and marketing as much as by new features.

background_read: Apple has introduced new iPhones every September since the first iPhone went on sale in 2007, and the launch event has become one of the tech world's biggest annual rituals.

The 'Pro' label first appeared on an iPhone in 2019, when Apple sold the iPhone 11 alongside two Pro versions in the same season — a pattern it has repeated almost every year since, which is what makes a missing standard model so unusual.

Foldable phones are not brand-new technology: Samsung and other Android makers have sold bendable-screen models since 2019, while Apple stayed out of that market until this event, so the 'passport-shaped' iPhone Duo marks a genuine change in strategy.

Two of the sources named in the article are The Information (a subscription tech-news outlet known for inside reporting on large technology firms) and MacRumors (a long-running website that tracks Apple rumours and leaks), while Counterpoint Research (a market-research firm that measures device sales) provided the sales figure.

The 'component crunch' mentioned is a real and broader pattern: the boom in AI computing has pushed up demand for memory chips and other parts, and those higher costs often reach shoppers as higher prices — one reason phone makers increasingly sell fewer, more expensive models to protect their profits.

perspectives.description: From this angle the event delivered real innovation: a first foldable in the iPhone Duo, better AI performance and a smarter Dynamic Island with up to three apps. Splitting the year across two events means each product gets attention instead of being buried in a crowded September stream, and buyers who want the best are willing to pay $1,199 or more.

The people who buy the standard iPhone, the best-selling model, got nothing new and must either wait until spring or buy a year-old iPhone 17. Meanwhile the Pro models rose $100, part of an AI-driven component crunch pushing prices upward, so the delay looks less like a gift of choice and more like premium customers being served first.

Apple has long staggered its releases, using separate events for lower-cost or mid-cycle models, and with six iPhones to sell it makes commercial sense to spread them out. Delaying the standard model also protects profit margins while memory and component costs climb, and it avoids the standard phone undercutting the Pros during the highest-spending weeks of the year.

The spring event will reveal whether the iPhone 18, a possible iPhone Air 2 or an iPhone 18e arrive as promised, and whether foldable designs become a permanent part of the lineup after the Duo. The bigger question is whether AI-related costs keep pushing phone prices up, and whether buyers eventually push back by holding onto their devices longer.
